demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She was sixty-six years old, but her face still worked—that was the way she put it. For forty years, her face had been her living: the high cheekbones, the pale blue eyes that tilted slightly upward, the mouth that could arrange itself into any emotion the camera required. She had modeled everything from foundation garments to luxury automobiles. In her late fifties, she had transitioned gracefully into “mature elegance” campaigns. She knew how to hold a pose, how to make stillness seem like breath.

The accident happened three years ago, on a two-lane road in upstate New York. She had been driving home from a shoot—a catalog for cashmere sweaters, shot in an old barn. She remembers the light, the way the October afternoon threw long, golden shadows across the asphalt. She remembers reaching for her phone. Not to look at it—just to move it from the passenger seat into her bag, because it kept sliding off the leather. One second her hand was fumbling, the next the wheel jerked. There was a sound she can still hear in her sleep: a dull, wet thump, followed by metal scraping against metal. She had clipped a cyclist, a man in his late thirties, a high school biology teacher out for a Saturday ride. He had been thrown onto the hood and then into the ditch.

She stopped. She called 911. She held his hand while they waited, his face a mask of blood and gravel. She remembers saying, “You’re going to be okay, you’re going to be okay,” over and over, even though she did not believe it. The paramedics told her later that if she had been going five miles per hour faster, he would have died. As it was, he suffered a traumatic brain injury, a shattered pelvis, and the loss of his spleen. He spent four months in rehabilitation. He will never teach again.

She was not charged. The police report noted distracting driving, but no impairment. The cyclist’s family never sued. They were kind, in a way that makes her feel worse. She wrote them letters. She visited the man once, in the hospital. He did not remember her. His wife said, “He doesn’t hold any blame.” But the patient—let us call her Diane—holds it all.

In the early months after the accident, Diane could not stop replaying it. The thump, the screech, the silence. She would be in the middle of a shoot, holding a silk scarf just so, and the light would shift and she would see the man’s face instead. Her hands would begin to tremble. The photographers learned to work around it; they are patient with her, because she is still a legend in the industry. But she has stopped taking jobs that require her to drive anywhere unfamiliar. She takes the train. She asks for rides. She will not get behind the wheel on a two-lane road.

She stopped driving altogether six months ago. It was not a decision; it was a refusal of her body. She would sit in her car, hands on the wheel, and begin to shake. Her heart would pound so hard that she thought she was having a heart attack. She would see the cyclist’s body, the way his arm bent backward. She would think: I did that. My hands. My choice to move the phone.

She is widowed, thirteen years now. Her husband died of a heart attack in their kitchen. She grieved him, but that grief had edges; it softened over time. This grief has no edges. It is a pit. She wakes at four in the morning and lies still, listening for the sound of the thump. She checks the news for his name. She wonders if he is in pain today. She wonders if he dreams of bicycles.

At shoots, she is still professional. She can smile, she can gaze, she can brood on command. But between shots, she stands apart, her arms crossed, watching the light. She does not talk about what happened. She does not talk about the cyclist. She says, “I’m fine,” when anyone asks. But at night, alone in her house, she sits in the dark and counts the ways she could undo it, none of them possible.
